prompt:
There are $800$ marbles in a bag. Each marble is colored with one of $100$ colors, and there are eight marbles of each color. Anna draws one marble at a time from the bag, without replacement, until she gets eight marbles of the same color, and then she immediately stops.

Suppose Anna has not stopped after drawing $699$ marbles. Compute the probability that she stops immediately after drawing the $700$th marble.

solutions.title: Look at the marbles left
solutions.body:
After $699$ draws without stopping, each color has been drawn at most $7$ times, so each color has at least $1$ marble left. The $101$ remaining marbles are therefore: one color with $2$ marbles left and $99$ colors with exactly $1$ left.

Anna stops on the next draw exactly when she draws a color that has only one marble left (she then has all $8$ of it). Each of the $101$ remaining marbles is equally likely, and $99$ of them work.

**Answer: $\frac{99}{101}$**

solutions.title: Count the bad outcomes
solutions.body:
The only way not to stop is to draw one of the $2$ marbles of the color that still has two left (she would then have only $7$ of that color). So the probability of not stopping is $\frac{2}{101}$, and the probability of stopping is $1-\frac2{101}=\frac{99}{101}$.

**Answer: $\frac{99}{101}$**

prompt: Compute the number of ways to tile a $3\times5$ rectangle with one $1\times1$ tile, one $1\times2$ tile, one $1\times3$ tile, one $1\times4$ tile, and one $1\times5$ tile. (The tiles can be rotated, and tilings that differ by rotation or reflection are considered distinct.)

solutions.title: Place the long tiles first
solutions.body:
The $1\times5$ and $1\times4$ tiles cannot stand vertically (the height is $3$), so the $1\times5$ fills a whole row and the $1\times4$ lies in another row, leaving one cell of that row empty. Split by the row of the $1\times5$:

- **Top row.** The other two rows form a $2\times5$ region. The $1\times4$ has $4$ placements (middle or bottom row, at the left or right end). The empty cell beside it is filled by the $1\times1$ or by a vertical $1\times2$ (2 choices); in each case the remaining $4$ or $5$ cells of the other row take the last two tiles in $2$ orders. Total $4\cdot2\cdot2=16$.
- **Middle row.** The top and bottom rows are separate $1\times5$ strips, so all tiles are horizontal: one strip holds the $1\times4$ and $1\times1$, the other the $1\times3$ and $1\times2$. Choose the strip for the $1\times4$ ($2$), and the order in each strip ($2\cdot2$): $8$.
- **Bottom row.** Mirror image of the first case: $16$.

Total $16+8+16=40$.

**Answer: 40**

solutions.title: Exhaustive search
solutions.body:
A backtracking search (fill the first empty cell with each unused tile, horizontally or vertically) counts exactly $40$ tilings.

**Answer: 40**

prompt: Richard starts with the string $\mathtt{HHMMMMTT}$. A move consists of replacing an instance of $\mathtt{HM}$ with $\mathtt{MH}$, replacing an instance of $\mathtt{MT}$ with $\mathtt{TM}$, or replacing an instance of $\mathtt{TH}$ with $\mathtt{HT}$. Compute the number of possible strings he can end up with after performing zero or more moves.

solutions.title: The M positions decide everything
solutions.body:
An H and a T can only swap via $\mathtt{TH}\to\mathtt{HT}$, which needs a T to the left of an H. Initially every H is left of every T, and no move can put a T left of an H, so that move never happens. Hence the H's stay in order before the T's, and only M's move (left past H's, right past T's).

So a reachable string is determined by the positions of the four M's: the remaining four places read HHTT from left to right. Conversely every choice of M positions is reachable: move the M's one at a time to their targets, using $\mathtt{HM}\to\mathtt{MH}$ to move an M left past an H and $\mathtt{MT}\to\mathtt{TM}$ to move it right past a T. Therefore the count is $\binom84=70$.

**Answer: 70**

solutions.title: Search
solutions.body:
A breadth-first search from $\mathtt{HHMMMMTT}$ applying all allowed moves reaches exactly $70$ strings.

**Answer: 70**

prompt: The cells of a $5\times5$ grid are each colored red, white, or blue. Sam starts at the bottom-left cell of the grid and walks to the top-right cell by taking steps one cell either up or to the right. Thus, he passes through $9$ cells on his path, including the start and end cells. Compute the number of colorings for which Sam is guaranteed to pass through a total of exactly $3$ red cells, exactly $3$ white cells, and exactly $3$ blue cells no matter which route he takes.

solutions.title: Anti-diagonals are monochromatic
solutions.body:
Let $c_{i,j}$ be the cell in row $i$ from the bottom and column $j$ from the left.

**Claim.** For $1\le i,j<5$, cells $c_{i+1,j}$ and $c_{i,j+1}$ have the same color. Take a path $P$ from $c_{1,1}$ to $c_{i,j}$ and a path $Q$ from $c_{i+1,j+1}$ to $c_{5,5}$. The routes $P\to c_{i+1,j}\to Q$ and $P\to c_{i,j+1}\to Q$ differ only in that one cell, and both must have three cells of each color, so the two cells match.

Thus each diagonal $D_k=\{c_{a,b}:a+b=k\}$, $k=2,\dots,10$, is one color. Every route meets each $D_k$ exactly once, so the condition becomes: among the $9$ diagonals, $3$ are red, $3$ white, $3$ blue. Conversely any such coloring works. The count is
$$\binom{9}{3,3,3}=\frac{9!}{3!\,3!\,3!}=1680.$$

**Answer: 1680**

solutions.title: Why constant diagonals are forced, informally
solutions.body:
Two routes that differ by a single 'corner flip' (right-then-up versus up-then-right) differ in exactly one cell each. Any two routes are connected by a chain of corner flips, and every pair of adjacent cells on a diagonal appears in some flip. So the coloring must be constant on diagonals, and it is just a coloring of the $9$ diagonals with three of each color: $\frac{9!}{(3!)^3}=1680$.

**Answer: 1680**

prompt:
Elbert and Yaiza each draw $10$ cards from a $20$-card deck with cards numbered $1,2,3,\dots,20$. Then, starting with the player with the card numbered $1$, the players take turns placing down the lowest-numbered card from their hand that is greater than every card previously placed. When a player cannot place a card, they lose and the game ends.

Given that Yaiza lost and $5$ cards were placed in total, compute the number of ways the cards could have been initially distributed. (The order of cards in a player's hand does not matter.)

solutions.title: Blocks of consecutive owners
solutions.body:
List the cards $1,\dots,20$ in order and mark each E or Y by owner. Split this string into maximal blocks of equal letters. Each player always plays their smallest card above the last card placed, which is exactly the first card of the next block; so the cards placed are the first cards of the blocks, the number of cards placed equals the number of blocks, and after the first card of the last block is placed the opponent has nothing higher and loses.

So we need exactly $5$ blocks, and since Yaiza lost, Elbert owns the last block. Blocks alternate, so the pattern is E Y E Y E: Elbert's $10$ cards form $3$ nonempty blocks and Yaiza's $10$ cards form $2$ nonempty blocks.
- Splitting Elbert's $10$ cards into $3$ nonempty consecutive groups: $\binom92=36$ ways.
- Splitting Yaiza's $10$ cards into $2$ nonempty groups: $\binom91=9$ ways.

Total $36\cdot9=324$.

**Answer: 324**

solutions.title: Brute force
solutions.body:
Simulating the game for all $\binom{20}{10}=184756$ distributions and counting those in which exactly $5$ cards are placed and Yaiza loses gives $324$.

**Answer: 324**

prompt: Each cell of a $3\times3$ grid is labeled with a digit in the set $\{1,2,3,4,5\}$. Then, the maximum entry in each row and each column is recorded. Compute the number of labelings for which every digit from $1$ to $5$ is recorded at least once.

solutions.title: Place entries from largest to smallest
solutions.body:
There are $6$ records (3 rows, 3 columns) and $5$ required values, so exactly one value is recorded twice.

- **The 5.** Every 5 is the maximum of its row and of its column. Two 5's would produce at least $3$ records of $5$, leaving too few for $1,2,3,4$. So there is exactly one 5 ($9$ positions), recorded twice; the other $4$ lines must record $1,2,3,4$ once each.
- **The 4.** A 4 outside the 5's row and column would be recorded twice. A 4 in the 5's row is recorded by its column; two 4's would give two records of 4. So there is exactly one 4, in line with the 5: $4$ positions.

Say the 5 and 4 are in row $R_1$, columns $C_1$ and $C_2$. The lines $R_2$, $R_3$, $C_3$ must record $1,2,3$ once each. All other cells are at most $3$.

- **Cell $(R_1,C_3)=3$.** Then $C_3$ records $3$, so rows $R_2,R_3$ contain only 1's and 2's and must record $1$ and $2$: one row all 1's, the other containing a 2: $2(2^3-1)=14$ ways.
- **Cell $(R_1,C_3)\in\{1,2\}$.** A 3 in column $C_3$ would be recorded by its row and by $C_3$, so the 3's lie in columns $C_1,C_2$ of one row $R_a$ only ($2$ choices of row; its two cells take values in $\{1,2,3\}$ with at least one 3: $9-4=5$ ways). The other row $R_b$ and column $C_3$ must record $1$ and $2$:
  - $C_3$ all 1's, $R_b$ has a 2 among its first two cells: $3$ ways;
  - $R_b$ all 1's, and one of the other two cells of $C_3$ is a 2: $3$ ways.

  This gives $2\cdot5\cdot(3+3)=60$.

Total $9\cdot4\cdot(14+60)=2664$.

**Answer: 2664**

solutions.title: Exhaustive check
solutions.body:
There are only $5^9\approx2\times10^6$ labelings. Checking each one by computer (compute the $6$ row/column maxima, test that all of $1,\dots,5$ appear) gives exactly $2664$.

**Answer: 2664**

prompt:
Svitlana writes the number $147$ on a blackboard. Then, at any point, if the number on the blackboard is $n$, she can perform one of the following three operations:
- if $n$ is even, she can replace $n$ with $\frac n2$;
- if $n$ is odd, she can replace $n$ with $\frac{n+255}2$; and
- if $n\ge64$, she can replace $n$ with $n-64$.

Compute the number of possible values that Svitlana can obtain by doing zero or more operations.

solutions.title: Think in 8-bit binary
solutions.body:
Write numbers as $8$-bit strings. $147=10010011_2$ has four 1's.

- If $n$ is even, $n/2$ rotates the $8$ bits right (the last bit $0$ moves to the front). If $n$ is odd, $\frac{n+255}{2}=\frac{n-1}2+128$ also rotates right (the last bit $1$ moves to the front). So the first two operations are cyclic rotations.
- $n-64$ (for $n\ge64$) changes the first two bits $11\to10$, $10\to01$, $01\to00$.

None of these increases the number of 1's, and all values stay below $2^8$. So every reachable value is an $8$-bit number with at most four 1's.

Conversely, every such number is reachable: rotations plus the move $10\to01$ in the first two bits let us swap any adjacent $10$ into $01$ anywhere, which (with rotations) rearranges the 1's into any positions; and rotating a 1 into the second position and applying $01\to00$ removes a 1. So all $8$-bit numbers with at most four 1's are reachable:
$$\binom80+\binom81+\binom82+\binom83+\binom84=1+8+28+56+70=163.$$

**Answer: 163**

solutions.title: Search
solutions.body:
A graph search from $147$ applying the three operations reaches exactly $163$ distinct values.

**Answer: 163**

prompt: A random permutation $a=(a_1,a_2,\dots,a_{40})$ of $(1,2,\dots,40)$ is chosen, with all permutations being equally likely. William writes down a $20\times20$ grid of numbers $b_{ij}$ such that $b_{ij}=\max(a_i,a_{j+20})$ for all $1\le i,j\le20$, but then forgets the original permutation $a$. Compute the probability that, given the values of $b_{ij}$ alone, there are exactly $2$ permutations $a$ consistent with the grid.

solutions.title: Peel off the largest value
solutions.body:
Think of $a_1,\dots,a_{20}$ as labels of rows and $a_{21},\dots,a_{40}$ as labels of columns, so $b_{ij}$ is the larger of the row label and the column label. The largest entry $m$ of the grid fills an entire row or an entire column, and that line's label must be $m$. Delete that line and repeat.

This determines everything until one side has a single line left. Then the remaining grid is $1\times k$; all its entries equal the label $L$ of the single line if $L$ is larger than the others, and the other $k$ labels are $\{1,\dots,k+1\}\setminus\{L\}$ arranged in any order. Concretely:
- if $1$ and $2$ are on different sides, the process ends with a $1\times1$ grid with entry $2$: the labels $1,2$ can be swapped, giving exactly $2$ permutations;
- if $1,2$ are on the same side and $3$ on the other, it ends with a $1\times2$ grid of 3's: $2!=2$ permutations;
- if $1,2,3$ are on the same side, it ends with a $1\times k$ grid with $k\ge3$: at least $3!=6$ permutations.

So we need $1,2,3$ not all on the same side. Given $1$'s side, $2$ is on the same side with probability $\frac{19}{39}$, and then $3$ too with probability $\frac{18}{38}$. The answer is
$$1-\frac{19}{39}\cdot\frac{18}{38}=1-\frac3{13}=\frac{10}{13}.$$

**Answer: $\frac{10}{13}$**

solutions.title: Small-case check
solutions.body:
The same reasoning for a $3\times3$ grid (permutations of $1,\dots,6$) predicts $1-\frac25\cdot\frac14=\frac9{10}$. Enumerating all $720$ permutations by computer and grouping them by grid confirms that exactly $90\%$ of permutations lie in groups of size $2$. For $20\times20$: $1-\frac{19\cdot18}{39\cdot38}=\frac{10}{13}$.

**Answer: $\frac{10}{13}$**

prompt: There are $100$ people standing in a line from left to right. Half of them are randomly chosen to face right (with all $\binom{100}{50}$ possible choices being equally likely), and the others face left. Then, while there is a pair of people who are facing each other and have no one between them, the leftmost such pair leaves the line. Compute the expected number of people remaining once this process terminates.

solutions.title: Minimum prefix sum and reflection
solutions.body:
Give right-facers weight $+1$ and left-facers $-1$ (so $2n=100$ people, total sum $0$). Removing an adjacent R…L pair (an "RL" pair) removes a $+1$ followed by $-1$, which does not change the minimum prefix sum. The final line has no RL, so it is $\mathtt{L}^k\mathtt{R}^k$, with minimum prefix sum $-k$ and $2k$ people. Hence the number remaining is $-2\cdot(\text{minimum prefix sum})$ of the original string (also, the order of removals does not matter).

By symmetry (swap R and L), $E[-\min]=E[\max]=\sum_{k\ge1}\Pr[\max\ge k]$. Viewing the string as a walk from $(0,0)$ to $(2n,0)$, reflecting the part after the first visit to height $k$ gives a bijection with walks ending at height $2k$, so $\Pr[\max\ge k]=\binom{2n}{n-k}/\binom{2n}{n}$. Then
$$\sum_{k\ge1}\binom{2n}{n-k}=\frac12\left(2^{2n}-\binom{2n}n\right),$$
so the expected number remaining is
$$2\cdot\frac{\frac12\left(2^{2n}-\binom{2n}n\right)}{\binom{2n}n}=\frac{2^{2n}}{\binom{2n}n}-1.$$
With $n=50$: $\dfrac{2^{100}}{\binom{100}{50}}-1\approx11.56$.

**Answer: $\dfrac{2^{100}}{\binom{100}{50}}-1$**

solutions.title: Check small cases
solutions.body:
For $2n$ people with $n=2,3,4,5$, enumerating all arrangements (and reducing the line with a stack) gives expected values $\frac53,\frac{11}5,\frac{93}{35},\frac{193}{63}$, which equal $\frac{4^n}{\binom{2n}n}-1$ in each case. So for $n=50$ the answer is $\frac{2^{100}}{\binom{100}{50}}-1$.

**Answer: $\dfrac{2^{100}}{\binom{100}{50}}-1$**

prompt: Let $x_0=x_{101}=0$. The numbers $x_1,x_2,\dots,x_{100}$ are chosen at random from the interval $[0,1]$ uniformly and independently. Compute the probability that $2x_i\ge x_{i-1}+x_{i+1}$ for all $i=1,2,\dots,100$.

solutions.title: Concave sequences and sorted differences
solutions.body:
Let $n=100$ and $A_i=(i,x_i)$. The condition says the points $A_0,\dots,A_{n+1}$ form a concave chain; almost surely it has a unique highest point $A_i$.

Left of the peak, the $i$ differences $x_1-x_0,\dots,x_i-x_{i-1}$ must be positive and decreasing. Given the multiset of values, almost surely: the $i-1$ values $x_1,\dots,x_{i-1}$ must be increasing (probability $\frac1{(i-1)!}$), and then the $i$ differences must be in decreasing order (probability $\frac1{i!}$, by a measure-preserving rearrangement of the differences). So the left part works with probability $\frac1{(i-1)!\,i!}$; similarly the right part with $\frac1{(n-i)!\,(n+1-i)!}$. Each index is equally likely to be the peak, so the probability is
$$\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\frac1{(i-1)!\,i!\,(n-i)!\,(n+1-i)!}=\frac1{n\cdot n!^2}\sum_{i=1}^n\binom n{i-1}\binom n{n-i}=\frac1{n\cdot n!^2}\binom{2n}{n-1}$$
by Vandermonde. For $n=100$: $\dfrac{1}{100\cdot100!^2}\dbinom{200}{99}$.

**Answer: $\dfrac{1}{100\cdot100!^2}\dbinom{200}{99}$**

solutions.title: Monte Carlo check of the formula
solutions.body:
The general formula $\frac{1}{n\cdot n!^2}\binom{2n}{n-1}$ gives $\frac12,\ \frac{15}{108}\approx0.1389,\ \frac{56}{2304}\approx0.0243$ for $n=2,3,4$. Simulating $2$ million random tuples for each $n$ gives $0.4999$, $0.1386$, $0.0242$ — a match. Substituting $n=100$ gives the answer.

**Answer: $\dfrac{1}{100\cdot100!^2}\dbinom{200}{99}$**
